claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability at high temperatures because high configurational entropy suppresses segregation and phase separation.
High configurational entropy increases atomic diffusion barriers.
The nanoparticles initially form a solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
High-energy ball milling or rapid quenching can enhance mixing and maximize configurational entropy.
Introducing slight local compositional inhomogeneity reduces local configurational entropy.
Suppression of local compositional fluctuations inhibits phase segregation.
A well-mixed state creates a larger barrier to atomic diffusion than a locally inhomogeneous state.
Larger atomic diffusion barriers reduce elemental migration and segregation during thermal stress.
Locally reduced mixing lowers diffusion barriers and thereby facilitates phase separation and chemical instability.
The maximally mixed nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than intentionally inhomogeneous nanoparticles under identical high-temperature histories.
The maximally mixed nanoparticles will exhibit less phase separation than intentionally inhomogeneous nanoparticles under identical high-temperature histories.
The maximally mixed nanoparticles will undergo fewer morphology changes and better preserve a single-phase solid solution.
Nanoparticles made using standard mixing protocols typically undergo some structural or chemical evolution during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Entropy stabilization is expected to dominate only within the specified service-temperature regimes.
Strong reactive atmospheres can override entropy stabilization through chemical driving forces such as preferential oxidation.
Slower cooling or pre-segregating thermochemical treatment can produce an intentionally inhomogeneous comparison batch.

contradictions.description: The intervention and falsification design specify a two-batch comparison between enhanced mixing and intentional inhomogeneity, whereas the baseline is separately defined as standard mixing. It is unclear whether standard mixing is a third control or whether the intentionally inhomogeneous batch is intended to serve as the baseline.
